summary: Sarah bears Isaac at the promised time, but after the weaning feast she demands Hagar and Ishmael be sent away so Ishmael will not share Isaac’s inheritance. Abraham sends them into the wilderness, where God hears the boy and provides water; later Abraham and Abimelech settle a dispute over a well and swear an oath at Beersheba.
whyItMatters: The long-awaited birth brings joy but also a desperate expulsion of another mother and child. The closing well treaty shows Abraham negotiating a foothold as a foreign resident rather than simply possessing the land.

context.author: Genesis names no historical writer. Jewish and Christian tradition associates the Torah with Moses; the book briefing describes older traditions shaped into a final literary form, without a settled account of every stage.
context.audience: The book addresses Israel through a story of shared human origins and the family from whom Israel traces its ancestry; no single first audience is named in this chapter.
context.date: The narrated events belong to primeval or ancestral time, not to a securely dated writing event. Major stages of Genesis are often placed across the monarchic to Persian periods, with exact models and dates debated.
context.setting: Abraham and Sarah’s household, the wilderness of Beersheba and Paran, and a disputed well.
context.literaryForm: Birth and weaning account, expulsion and rescue narrative, followed by an oath-and-well treaty.

before.text: God has restored Sarah after Abimelech took her and has promised her a son at an appointed time. This chapter begins with that birth.

here.text: Read Isaac’s birth and laughter beside Hagar and Ishmael’s expulsion, then follow the separate public dispute about Beersheba’s well.

after.text: God tests Abraham by commanding Isaac’s offering, and a ram is eventually provided in Isaac’s place.

outline.heading: Isaac born and celebrated
outline.note: Sarah bears Isaac, he receives the covenant sign, and his weaning is celebrated.

outline.heading: Sarah demands Hagar and Ishmael leave
outline.note: Inheritance conflict grieves Abraham; God names distinct futures for Isaac and Ishmael.

outline.heading: Water runs out; God hears the boy
outline.note: Hagar and Ishmael face death in the wilderness before a well and future are shown.

outline.heading: Abimelech requests an oath
outline.note: The ruler asks Abraham to treat his house and land truthfully.

outline.heading: Well dispute and Beersheba covenant
outline.note: They settle the well claim with animals and an oath; Abraham remains a foreigner.

keyVerses.text: Sarah said, “God has made me laugh. Everyone who hears will laugh with me.”
keyVerses.why: Sarah’s laughter marks the fulfilled birth promise in her own speech.

keyVerses.text: She went and sat down opposite him, a good way off, about a bow shot away. For she said, “Don’t let me see the death of the child.” She sat opposite him, and lifted up her voice, and wept.
keyVerses.why: Hagar’s fear of watching the child die gives the expulsion its human cost.

keyVerses.text: God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water. She went, filled the container with water, and gave the boy a drink.
keyVerses.why: The discovery of water is the immediate answer to the wilderness crisis.

questions.question: How does Isaac’s birth answer earlier promises?
questions.answer: Sarah conceives and bears a son at the set time God had named, and Abraham calls him Isaac and circumcises him on the eighth day. Sarah’s laughter now celebrates the birth rather than only its improbability.

questions.question: What happens when Sarah calls for Hagar and Ishmael to be cast out?
questions.answer: She wants Ishmael excluded from Isaac’s inheritance. Abraham is grieved but sends mother and child away with bread and water after God tells him to listen to Sarah, and their water later runs out in the wilderness.

questions.question: What does “weaned” mark in the opening?
questions.answer: It is the stage when Isaac no longer nurses, celebrated by Abraham with a feast. The chapter gives no exact age for Isaac then, so the later conflict cannot be dated precisely from the word alone.

questions.question: Does God forget Ishmael when Isaac becomes the named heir?
questions.answer: No. God says Ishmael too will become a nation because he is Abraham’s son, hears the boy in the wilderness, and remains with him as he grows. These promises do not erase the danger he and Hagar face after being sent away.

questions.question: Why is the child left under a shrub?
questions.answer: After the water runs out, Hagar places him there and moves away because she cannot bear to watch him die. The passage portrays desperation, not a casual abandonment, and God’s response is to direct her back to hold him and find water.

questions.question: What is Abraham’s dispute with Abimelech?
questions.answer: Abraham says Abimelech’s servants violently took a well he dug, while Abimelech says he had not heard of it. They make a covenant, and seven ewe lambs witness Abraham’s claim to the well.

questions.question: Why is the place called Beersheba?
questions.answer: The narrative connects the name with the oath Abraham and Abimelech swear there after settling the well claim. Abraham plants a tree and calls on Yahweh’s name at that place.

questions.question: Does Abraham’s well agreement mean he owns all surrounding land?
questions.answer: The agreement witnesses his claim to one dug well and his covenant with Abimelech. The chapter ends by saying Abraham remains a foreigner in the land of the Philistines, not a ruler over it.

glossary.def: No longer nursing, the life stage of Isaac marked with a feast.
The place named for the oath and well agreement between Abraham and Abimelech.
The seven female sheep set apart as witnesses to Abraham’s claim that he dug the well.
